title: 13 Percent of Indian Employees Face High Burnout as AI Threatens 20 Percent Job Cuts
excerpt: A Great Place To Work India study of 5.7 million employees finds persistent burnout, declining discretionary effort, and growing anxiety over AI-driven workforce reductions.
body:
• Around 13 percent of Indian employees report high-level burnout, a figure that has remained stubbornly stable since 2022, according to Great Place To Work India.
  • Nearly 25 percent of CHROs expect AI to reduce workforce headcount by 1–20 percent within the next two years, while 45 percent say it is too early to estimate the full impact.
  • Discretionary effort has fallen 4 percent since 2023, with six in ten organizations reporting year-on-year declines in employees' willingness to go beyond basic duties.
  • Gen Z now accounts for 26 percent of the Indian workforce, nearly double its share in 2023, with 81 percent of CHROs citing workplace flexibility as their top priority.

A sweeping study by Great Place To Work India, covering over 5.7 million employees across more than 20 industries, paints a sobering picture of India's corporate workforce: persistent burnout that refuses to improve, a growing anxiety around AI-driven job losses, and an "effort recession" where employees are increasingly unwilling to go the extra mile.

Burnout Has Plateaued, Not Improved

While medium burnout has dropped from 21 percent in 2019 to about 15 percent currently, overall burnout levels have stalled. Around 13 percent of employees continue to report high-level burnout — exhaustion severe enough to affect both work performance and daily life outside the office. Approximately 72 percent fall in the low-burnout category.

The improvement, in other words, peaked years ago. Between 2022 and 2026, the needle has barely moved despite increased corporate spending on wellness programs and mental health initiatives.

AI Is Creating a New Divide

AI adoption has moved well past the experimentation phase, but the transition is exposing deep fissures in the workplace. Around 44 percent of CHROs say high performers are pulling further ahead by leveraging AI tools effectively, while others struggle to keep pace. This creates what the study calls a new workplace divide — not between different skill levels, but between those who can use AI and those who cannot.

Trust is another casualty. About 32 percent of CHROs report that employees are unsure which AI-generated outputs need verification and which can be trusted. And 21 percent of managers say they do not know how to evaluate performance in an AI-enabled workplace.

"The challenge is not simply about adopting AI. It is about building confidence around how jobs, careers, performance and opportunities will change."

— Balbir Singh, CEO, Great Place To Work India

The bigger fear, however, is headcount. Nearly 25 percent of CHROs anticipate a 1–20 percent workforce reduction due to AI over the next two years. Almost 45 percent say it is too early to estimate the full impact, while 26 percent of employees feel leadership is not clearly addressing job security concerns.

The Effort Recession

Beyond burnout and AI anxiety, a quieter trend is reshaping Indian workplaces: declining discretionary effort. The study found a 4 percent drop since 2023, with six in ten organizations reporting year-on-year declines. Employees are still doing their jobs, but fewer are willing to go beyond the minimum.

Nearly 58 percent of CHROs say they are dealing with AI disruption and generational workforce challenges simultaneously. Half admit they do not clearly understand what motivates younger employees.

Gen Z Is Reshaping Expectations

Gen Z now makes up 26 percent of the Indian workforce, nearly twice its share in 2023. Their participation has surged an average of 16 percent over the past four years across every major industry. This cohort is bringing fundamentally different expectations: 81 percent of CHROs say workplace flexibility is Gen Z's top priority, compared to just 8 percent for Gen X and older generations.

The generational shift is creating friction around career growth models, employee engagement strategies and what it means to be motivated at work.

What Companies Can Do

The study points to trust as the critical differentiator. Organizations with strong leadership confidence see a 47 percent increase in productivity, a 56 percent boost in agility and 34 percent higher innovation. The message for employers is clear: AI adoption without transparency, training and genuine communication about job security will accelerate both burnout and attrition.
